1:
Four months lie between the news and the request, and the delay is accounted for differently. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) will not have it look like idleness: Nehemiah did not sit still and say, Let God now do his own work, for I have no more to do, but set himself to forecast what he could do towards it — our prayers must be seconded with our serious endeavours, else we mock God. John Gill (reformed) puts two possibilities, that he purposely spent the time in fasting and prayer, or that until now his turn did not come round to wait upon the king as cupbearer. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) supplies a mechanism for the second, supposing the Persian kings kept a different cup-bearer for each quarter of the year and that it had just come to Nehemiah’s turn. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) leaves both standing: either his turn did not come till then, or till then he wanted a fit opportunity to move it.

What exactly he feared is disputed. Clarke reads the king’s question as suspicion, as though Artaxerxes thought his servant harboured some bad design and read treachery or remorse in his face. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) locates it in protocol: for three months Nehemiah had discharged his duties without being sad in the king’s presence, a sad countenance was never tolerated there, and though Artaxerxes was of a milder character than any other Persian monarch, the tone of the abrupt inquiry showed he was no exception in this. Wesley puts the danger further off, among the courtiers, the request being great and invidious and odious to most of them, so that what he feared was disappointment. Henry offers two more: the king’s wrath, those eastern monarchs assuming an absolute power of life and death, or else misplacing a word and losing the request by mismanaging it.

The plea itself is read as a calculation. Ellicott observes that Nehemiah does not yet betray the deepest desire of his heart but speaks only of the desecration of his fathers’ sepulchres, an appeal of great force with Persians, who respected the tomb. Clarke agrees on the force and generalises it, the tombs of the dead being sacred among the ancients and nothing more detestable than disturbing their remains, so that Nehemiah knew the circumstance would strongly interest the feelings of the Persian king. Wesley notices what the plea leaves out — he says not a word of the temple, speaking as he was before a heathen king who cared for none of these things. Gill hears the opening salutation the same way, that some think the wish that the king live for ever was meant to take off any suspicion of a design on his life, though it seems a common salutation of those times.

The queen sitting by is noticed by all and identified by no two alike. Clarke denies she was a queen at all, taking shegal to mean rather a concubine or chief favourite, which the Septuagint renders as harlot, and denies she was Esther. Ellicott makes her Damaspia, the one legitimate queen, and infers from her presence that this was no public feast, since at such a feast she would not have appeared. Gill guesses Atossa the daughter of Cyrus, who might be the friendlier to the Jews on her father’s account, and notes that it was not common for Persian queens to dine with their husbands at all. Henry declines to settle whether she was his back friend, who would have hindered him, or his true friend, present to help the request forward, and takes the uncertainty for the point: Nehemiah credits neither her nor his own standing, but the good hand of his God upon him. Clarke draws the same line, that he might have pleaded long and faithful service, and would not.
9:
The escort is weighed against a precedent. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads the captains and horsemen two ways at once, as a guard and as a public honour, to show that he was a man whom the king did delight to honour, that all the king’s servants might respect him accordingly; those whom the King of kings sends, he adds, he thus protects. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) set the same detail beside Ezra, who had been ashamed to request a military escort of the Persian monarch, where Nehemiah as a high dignitary was simply given a guard of soldiers, and they judge that the guard stayed on with him in Jerusalem for his protection. John Gill (reformed) leaves the governors themselves unidentified, declining to say whether they were the same Tatnai and Shetharboznai who had held the office eighteen years before.

What Sanballat’s title means is a real quarrel. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) makes him probably a native of Horonaim, a Moabite by birth and now governor of the Samaritans under the king of Persia; Gill allows that he either presided at Horonaim or sprang from it, a city of Moab, and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) names the same eminent Moabite city as his birthplace or seat of rule. Keil and Delitzsch reject that reading outright, and on a grammatical ground: he is certainly not from Horonaim in Moab, as older expositors imagined, since he would then have been called a Moabite, but from the upper or the nether Beth-horon, once of Ephraim and in Nehemiah’s day within the Samaritan region. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) follows them to one of the Beth-horons, now in the kingdom of Samaria, and observes that the name itself looks Babylonian while Tobiah’s is Hebrew.

The second title divides them as sharply. Keil and Delitzsch take Tobiah to be called the servant probably as an official of the Persian king. Ellicott demotes him to Sanballat’s own secretary or minister. Clarke promotes him instead to joint governor alongside Sanballat under the Persian king, and adds that some suppose this Sanballat to be the man who later persuaded Alexander to build a temple on Mount Gerizim, Pelagius thinking rather that there were two governors of the name. Wesley reads the word as a record of origin rather than office, so called probably from the condition out of which he had been raised to power, which he offers as a reason for the insolence that follows, it being usual for persons suddenly raised from a low state so to demean themselves.

Why the news should grieve them is pressed by two. Keil and Delitzsch notice that the grief is reported with irony, Nehemiah speaking from his enemies’ point of view when he says that a man was come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel. Henry supplies the motive: nothing is a greater vexation to the enemies of good people, who have misrepresented them to princes as turbulent and factious and not fit to live, than to see them stand right in the opinion of their rulers, their innocency cleared and their reproach rolled away, and to find them thought not merely fit to live but fit to be trusted. Ellicott puts it in plainer political terms, that the revival of Jerusalem would be a blow to the recent ascendency of Samaria.
11:
The three days’ rest and the silence that follows are given more than one motive. John Gill (reformed) has him resting from the fatigue of the journey and receiving the visits of his friends, as Ezra had done before him, and Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) adds devotion to the rest, again after Ezra’s example. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) explain the secrecy by the opposition already met: knowing the hostility of Sanballat and Tobiah, he would speak of his purpose to no one until an inspection of the wall had told him the magnitude of the work and made him certain it could be done. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) makes the point defensive, that he hid everything he could from their enemies until all was in readiness, lest they take measures to defeat the work. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) finds a second motive the others do not: he would not seem to act for ostentation, and if he found the thing impracticable he might retreat the more honourably.

The night route is traced by all four and agreed by none. Keil and Delitzsch put the valley-gate at or near the present Jaffa gate, opening west towards the valley of Gihon, and reckon the dragon-well, named only here, either the well of Gihon itself or its immediate neighbour. Ellicott turns the same gate south, opening on Hinnom, and says the dragon-well is nowhere else mentioned and not now to be traced at all. Clarke declines the topography and explains the name instead, as perhaps taken from a carved dragon out of whose mouth the stream issued from the well; the dung port he places on the eastern side, the way by which the city’s filth was carried into the valley of Hinnom. Keil and Delitzsch set that gate much farther south, near the pool of Siloah, against the tradition that finds it elsewhere; Gill reads the valley-gate as leading rather to the valley of dead bodies, through which Kidron ran.

The king’s pool divides them again. Keil and Delitzsch identify it with the pool Josephus calls Solomon’s and places east of the spring of Siloah, which Robinson and Thenius take for the present Fountain of the Virgin — an identification they report Bertheau as rightly objecting to. Clarke makes it not a pool but a work of engineering, probably the aqueduct Hezekiah made to bring the waters of Gihon to the city of David. Ellicott simply equates it with the fountain-gate of Siloah, and Gill, citing Rauwolff, notes that the gate of the fountain was still standing outside the Tyropaeum valley, so named because it led towards Siloah. On why the beast could go no further they are of one mind, John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) putting it most briefly: the way was obstructed with heaps of rubbish.

Who was kept in the dark is a question of titles. Keil and Delitzsch separate the nobles, as heads of the houses of the people, from the rulers, who are the town authorities, and explain that the builders are called the remnant by comparison with priests and rulers. Gill takes the rulers for officers of the king of Persia, precisely because the next clause distinguishes them from the Jewish rulers. Ellicott reads the work as still to come and justifies the caution from what followed, the city teeming with elements of danger while the nobles and rulers possessed no substantial repressive authority; Wesley glosses the same phrase as those whom Nehemiah intended to employ.
17:
The appeal is admired for what it does not do. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) presses the manner of it: Nehemiah did not undertake the work without them, nor charge and command imperiously though he had the king’s commission, but in a friendly brotherly way exhorted and excited them to join him, and took no praise to himself, acknowledging rather that God had put the thing into his heart. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read the two things he produced as calculated to gain the assembly’s regard, the hand which his God had graciously provided for him and the king’s own words, of which the narrative had so far reported only the order to the keeper of the forest. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that the opening word carries no note of time at all, and has him wait until his plans were matured before appealing to their patriotism. John Gill (reformed) itemises the providence: his exaltation in the Persian court, the opportunity to lay the case before the king, and the inclining of the king’s heart.

The answer of the assembly draws a lesson about leadership. Henry observes that they had all seen the desolations of Jerusalem and none of them had proposed the repair, but when one man proposed it they consented at once — many a good work would find hands enough to be laid to it if there were but one good head to lead in it, and it is a pity a good motion should be lost for want of someone to move it and break the ice. He adds that by stirring up ourselves and one another we strengthen ourselves and one another, the great reason for weakness in duty being coldness towards it. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) hears resolution in the words themselves, that they would do it with vigour and diligence as men determined to go through with it, and takes the strengthened hands to be their own and one another’s.

The third adversary and his charge are differently placed. Gill allows that Geshem might be both an Arabian by birth and governor of some part of Arabia near Judea, and Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) likewise makes him a chief of the Arabs lying next to Samaria. Ellicott subordinates both of Sanballat’s colleagues to him instead: they were not independent chieftains, Tobiah being Sanballat’s servant and counsellor and Geshem probably the leader of an Arabian company mostly in his service. On the charge of rebellion the two part company. Clarke makes it tactical, said to raise jealousies in the king’s mind and induce him to recall his ordinance. Keil and Delitzsch make it mockery, the irony lying in this, that the accusers did not credit the Jews with power enough to build fortifications and so to be able to rebel at all; they note that Gashmu is the fuller form of the name.

The reply is measured by an older one. Clarke recalls that citizenship of Jerusalem was a high honour, closed to those not of the tribes of Israel, and that Zerubbabel had given the Samaritans the same answer. Ellicott reaches the same parallel independently and sharpens it: the closing words imply that these enemies, like those in Zerubbabel’s day, really wanted a share in the undertaking, and Nehemiah gives Zerubbabel’s answer but strengthens it, leaving them not even a place in the city’s memorials save one of shame. Keil and Delitzsch explain the term, that only members of the congregation, who may hope to live on in their descendants there, can be said to have a memorial in Jerusalem. Wesley divides it, no portion meaning no authority over us nor interest in our church and state, and no memorial meaning no monument of relation by birth or religion, nor of any kindness done to us or to the place.
